So, I am at one with the Prime Minister a3 far as this is concerned. I am at one with him in this respect also that I think that an expenditure of money designed for that purpose ought, in the main at least, to be under the control of our own parliament and that by making an appro, priation of that kind and attending to. the defence of our own coasts, by co-operation and co-ordination with the imperial naval forces, we would be rendering a Teal service in the defence of the empire and we would be doing our duty not only to Canada but to the empire as a whole.
My right hon. friend has spoken in very eloquent terms of the necessity of maintaining the integrity of the empire. We are all at one with him there, and there are just one or two observations that I desire to make in that regard. The first is that the loss of the control of the seas by the British fleet means the dismemberment of this great empire. Great Britain having once lost control of the seas it is impossible to conceive that this empire would longer survive. A world-wide empire such as ours; an empire which reaches out on every continent and spreads over every ocean can only be maintained by absolute naval supremacy. The moment a naval power arises which can effectively challenge the supremacy of Britain's navy that moment may the British empire be dismembered and that moment Canada may cease to be among the nations of that great empire. I am not one of those who look to see the integrity of the British empire menaced by the future independence of Canada. Like Sir John Macdonald, I was born a British subject, I shall remain a British subject, I hope to die a British subject. I trust the day will never come when the British flag will cease to float over this Canada of ours. But as has been eloquently said, Britain staggers under the too vast orb of her fate, and so it behooves us her children to decide how we can best assist the motherland to maintain control of the seas. It is not for us tonight to lay down the details of a scheme by which we can best co-operate towards that end, and I agree with the Prime Minister that we. should act in conjunction with and by the advice of the British Admiralty. They have experts at their command, they have the experience of the past to direct them, and these we have not. While I venture	to think	that a
system of torpedo boats and submarines	such as has been adopted
by the Commonwealth of Australia would be perhaps the most effective way in which we could assist Great Britain ip a stated policy of naval defence, yet I agree that the Canadian government ought to have the advice of the British Admiralty and lend it-



I do not desire to say anything more od this subject. I believe that the defence of our own shores and the protection of our own commerce is due to the self-respect which should fill the heart of every man in this country. You say that we may rest contented to depend for our naval defence on Great Britain. Well, if we have assumed the status of a nation in one respect, shall we adhere to the status of a Crown colony in other and still more important respects?
You speak of a Monroe doctrine, but that doctrine would not defend our coasts, our cities and our commerce from the attacks of any foe; and it is idle to suggest that we could, in the case of a great naval war, obtain any measure of comfort from the Monroe doctrine. But if we should depend on the Monroe doctrine, would it not, as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) well said this afternoon, reduce us to a position of vassalage as regards the great republic. That is not a condition or a policy in harmony with our self respect or with our ideals and status as a nation. We desire that this resolution should go out as the unanimous resolution of the parliament of Canada to the whole world, and I believe it may go out as a message which [DOT] will do much to keep the peace of the world in these days of uncertainty. It should go in such terms as would entitle the Canadian people to the gratitude of the empire and do much to restore to the people of this country that self respect in which, it seems to me, we have been somewhat lacking in these days when others have done so much, and we so little, for naval defence so absolutely essential to the integrity and the maintenance of our great empire.

I am sure, Mr. Speaker, there will be no word of complaint from any portion of the British empire at the tone in which this discussion has been carried out. It is recognized on both sides that the question is too important, not only to Canada but to the British empire, to be discussed in any party spirit. It certainly is one which must be discussed from the broadest national point of view and a solution of which must be sought, not merely acceptable to the government of the day, but to future governments, as governments change from time to time. _ There is very little difference in the opinions expressed regarding general conditions. There can be no doubt that great dangers always have, and always must, attend great empires; some of these dangers come from without, but the majority from within; and it is one of the pleasing features in the history of the British empire in modern times, that whenever her foreign relations have been covered with gloom, that gloom has been dispelled

by the brightness of the loyalty of her daughters. That loyalty has burst forth amid the deepest gloom as when a sable cloud turns forth her silver lining on the night. There can be no doubt as to the loyalty of Canada and of every other dominion of Great Britain to the empire, and the question resolves itself into this: What shall the various portions of the empire do in order to put themselves in such a position as to be able, at the critical moment and at the proper time, to render the greatest assistance to the mother country. In Canada it is generally recognized that there is no military spirit dominant in the country and very little in favour of military establishments, unless such military and naval establishments as are absolutely essential for our welfare and the defence of the empire. There are better investments we can make in behalf of the empire and of Canada than expenditure upon navies or greater military organizations in the immediate present. If Canada desires to become a great nation, a nation that shall be a tower of strength to the mother country, as well as a sure bulwark of defence to herself, I do not see what better policy she can pursue than that of husbanding her strength and resources and thus enabling herself to become a powerful factor in the British empire. Were we at present to engage in a naval programme what would we require to do? It would be necessary to take the money of our people and go outside the boundaries of the Dominion to spend it. It seems to me that it would be better for the government and parliament of the Dominion to sanction such aid to our steel and iron industries in the east and west as will make it possible to us in a few years to build our own navy. You can never induce the people of Canada to make contributions for expenditure of that kind outside her own limits. I venture to say that no greater danger could arise to the empire than would follow if we agreed annually to contribute to the British authorities either a battleship or sufficient money to build one. That would create friction and controversy between the mother country and Canada; and any arrangement whereby the control of the money contributed by us would be under the authority of British statesmen, and not shared in any way by Canada, would lead to such conflicts and difficulties between the mother country and the Dominion as would be a source of danger to the empire. I believe that the best policy for us to pursue is the one we are now following and from which I see no reason for departing. That is the policy of being ready, as the people of Canada are always ready, to furnish whatever they have that may be necessary for the defence

of the empire in times of need.	But
if we start at present into any vast naval or military outlay we shall so impede our growth that in the course of a very short time we will be of much less assistance to the empire than if we permitted our country to advance and prosper as she is doing now. I do noi think that there is at present anything so critical in British relations as to cause us to get excited. One of our greatest publicists has said that of all the nations in the world, there is none so governed by their humour as the English. He said that two hundred years ago, and it is not less true to-day, and it is pleasant and consoling to find that the Scotchmen who are to-day in the cabinet of Great Britain do not share the excitement of some of the music halls of London regarding the danger hovering over the empire at present. I listened with some regret to the exordium of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Foster), I could not but think that if some heathen had been listening to that address he would have thought that the hon. gentleman was a great high priest of pessimism performing the funeral rites of Christianity. It may be that wars will come, it may be that we cannot prevent the recurrence of warfare, but the people of Canada are inclined to peace, and the efforts of our public men should be directed not to inflaming passions among nations, not to arousing hostility but to endeavour to bring about that time when war will cease and be looked upon as a vanity out of date and battleships as a superannuated piece of folly.
To-day there is talk of danger of war between the two great nations of Germany and Great Britain-Great Britain, the greatest contributor to the liberty of mankind in a political sense; Germany, the greatest contributor to the liberty of mankind in an intellectual and philosophical sense. These are the two most advanced nations of the world and why to-day is there any danger of hostilities between these nations? Is the fault entirely on the part of Germany? Is it not due to a large extent to the fact that each of these two nations is abusing the other, that their papers are full of abuse and ridicule, the English making tun of German awkwardness and the German of English awkwardness, saying all sorts of witty and offensive things, instead of treating each other with courtesy and attempting to conduct themselves in such a way as to render impossible a war between the two nations. Richter said that Providence had given to the French the empire of the land, to the English the empire of the seas and to the Germans the empire-of the air. I do not think any one could expect that Germany would be satisfied with the empire of the air. It must be remembered that Ger-111J
many is a vast and important and a great people, one of the greatest peoples of the world to-day and there is no instance in the history of the world of a great nation such as the German nation tying itself up within the narrow confines of an empire like Germany of to-day and not seeking and succeeding in obtaining some outlet for its population. Great Britain to-day has an outlet in all its vast empire for its surplus population, and I do not believe that anything could be better than that Germany should obtain some such outlet for hers. I believe the object in the creation of the German navy is to obtain an outlet of that kind, but I am satisfied that that aim could be best obtained by negotiations with other nations. It is customary to condemn the Emperor of Germany. We all remember when he ascended the throne 21 years ago the prognostications of what was to occur; he was to be the troubler of Europe, he was to create war here, there and everywhere, and w'e all know that the very contrary has been the case. He has undoubtedly made, as he doubtless would admit, a few mistakes. I do not know if he had the chance again, whether he would write the Kruger telegram, but that has long passed by and surely there should be a statutory limitation in regard to faults of that kind. No one can view his career without recognizing that he is one of the greatest rulers of modern times. Naturally enough he seeks to build up and_ to advance the interests of his own empire. It is only a few weeks since the King of England visited Germany and 'was received with great enthusiasm not only by the Emperor but by the people of Germany. The English were so delighted to find the people of Berlin naming streets after His Majesty that they almost became German in their sentiments. Yet to-day the Emperor . of Germany is going to conquer the British empire !
I do not think the people of Canada will cease to be patriotic, but I am sure they will never become hysterical in their patriotism. I hope they will continue to keep erected above them in regard to this, as in regard to other matters, the banner of sound common sense, and in the discussion of this and every other question they will not overlook homely self-interest, coupled with a due regard to and a due sense of what is reasonable and what is right. It seems to me you might as well have asked the old settler cutting down hardwood trees in Ontario in the days of tomahawk and scalping knife, to buy a uniform and enroll himself in a regiment of soldiers to protect those hardwood trees as to expect Canada to give up the development of this country, its settlement and the working of its vast resources and to turn her energies to develop-ping a great military and naval strength. If that is ever done, if that is immediately

done in Canada, you will divert from Canada her greatest attraction for increased population.
I venture to assert that if Great Britain would adopt the policy of the old tribes, when migrations of natives began, of dividing up the population, and placing in each portion a number of the noble and ignoble, the rich and the poor and then drawing lots as to which should get out of the country, we would gladly take one of those portions, help to bring them to Canada and help to build up here a further bulwark of strength for the British empire. I believe that some such sane, sensible scheme as that would be a thousand times better for the British empire, would make Canada a stronger support of the British empire than spending money on Dreadnoughts and on the military fuss and feathers some people would like to see in this country. The people of Canada will not submit to the drums and tramplings of militarism. They are going to defend themselves, but they are prepared to take some risk. Every man has to take the risk of loss of life or prop-perty; any one of us may be assassinated, but still the authorities will not allow us to carry guns for our own protection, and why cannot a large nation like the British or the Canadian take a certain risk? I would sooner be conquered by any people than go along as some people in London would have us, frightened to death that some foreign nation will conquer us. Even if Great Britain should lose her navy, and be in such a position that the New Zealander could stand on London bridge and view the remains of this old Dreadnought grounded on the Thames,
I do not believe that Canada would be in the slightest danger from any foreign aggression.
Oh, oh.

I hope that hon. gentlemen do not think I am prophesying any such disaster as that. If the hon. gentlemen in dissenting from my views thought that I was speaking of such a calamity as likely to occur to Great Britain, they misunderstood me. I was merely quoting Lord Macaulay's expression regarding the New Zealander standing upon the ruins of London bridge. Any reader of history knows that such disasters have occurred to the greatest empires. There are elements of strength and greatness in the British empire, but they do not relieve it from the possibility of the fate that has pursued all great nations of the world from the Hittites down to the present day. But even if that disaster should occur, there is no danger to Canada if the proper policy is pursued in Canada, the policy of training every young man in the country in physical exercise, the train-

ing to which Lord Stratheona has devoted his magnificent gift. If every young man is taught to use the rifle, if every young man is taught discipline, you can in this way build up a population of free men, ready to lay down their lives in defence of their country, and we need not fear the Dutchmen or any one endeavouring to invade or conquer our country. You might as well talk about raising fortifications as a protection against the great republic to the south. We all know there is no danger of invasion from the southern republic. The spirit of that people is too far advanced; the danger of collision between them and us has, I believe, absolutely passed away, and when you begin to talk about military matters at our present stage of a material development, it is exactly as though a young boy, a recruit, should shove into a lot of gladiators showing his biceps and declaring that they could not get on without fighting. It is not necessary for Canada to talk about fighting, it is necessary for her to pursue a policy that will avoid difficulties and entanglements for the British empire and relieve her from the horrors and dangers of warfare. The ideal I have of Canada is not a country with fortifications here and there, and people listening to the drums and trampling of soldiers, with horrid, hideous battleships around our coasts. The ideal I have of Canada is a Canada that, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, shall contain no city in which there is a single slum, no city in which there are any of those abominations which to-day exist in other countries, and I say that to-day Canada would be pursuing a noble aim and a noble object and an object which would make her a great country, if she pursued the policy of endeavouring in every city to create a civic spirit, determined ' to see that the labouring class in that city should not be in want, that there should be in it none of those disreputable quarters which seem to be an inseparable auxiliary of the cities of the old world. -I do not know, Mr. Speaker, that there is the slightest danger of Canada going crazy over this question. I am quite convinced that we shall not build any Dreadnoughts in the near future, and send them over the water; but if we do I hope we will give her the usual bill of lading,
' God send the good ship safe to harbour,' and that no disasters will occur to Canada, in consequence, to force us hereafter to declare ' It was that fatal and perfidious bark built in the eclipse and rigged with curses dark that sunk so low that sacred head of thine.'

I have listened with a great deal of pleasure, as I usually do, to the speech of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) ; I have also listened with a great deal of pleasure to the eloquent speech delivered

by the right hon. the Prime Minister, and to the very able speech delivered by the leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Borden). I may also say that I have listened to the speech of the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Congdon) but I cannot say that I have listened to it with much pleasure. Judging from the hon. members speech, we have a right to conclude that he is going to vote both against the resolution of the hon. member for North Toronto and against the amendment of the Prime Minister. He has totally ignored the conditions that exist in the empire to-day. He has totally disregarded the fact that the statesmen of Great Britain, in the speeches they have delivered in the British House of Parliament, have declared that the time has arrived when the supremacy of the British navy is being menaced, that Germany has shown by her haste in the construction of battleships that she intends to challenge the supremacy of the British navy. The hon. gentleman has totally ignored these facts, and has shown by his speech that he is not in favour of any immediate action by 'Canada to give assistance to the motherland.
A great deal has been said for and against any concrete action being taken to render assistance to the mother land. Let me say a few words on that question,. We are here to-day to protect the Dominion of Canada a country that has a population of nearly seven millions, a country that is thirty-three times as large as Italy, eighteen times as large as Germany, eighteen times as large as France, nearly as large as the whole of Europe, and slightly larger than the United States. We are here to protect the commerce and the productiveness of the Dominion of Canada. We are here to protect 7,000 miles of coast line on the Pacific coast. We are here to protect the great industries of British Columbia with her total yearly production of $88,000,000 worth, her fisheries worth between six and seven millions, her mineral production amounting to twenty-three million dollars, her 13,000 men engaged in the fishing industry, and her 9,000 men engaged on the shore fisheries of that province. Then I pass over the Rocky mountains and come to the province of Alberta. We are here to protect the nineteen million bushels of grain that' are raised in that province, valued at ten and a half million dollars, and her three million dollars' worth of cattle exported from that province last year. Then I pass on into the province of Saskatchewan. We are here to protect the 105 million bushels of grain raised in that province during the last year, and valued at sixty million dollars. I pass onward into the province of Manitoba, and we are here to protect the 113 million bushels of grain raised there, of a value of something like fifty million dollars. I come down into the old province of Ontario with its many
agricultural products. We are here to protect the 185 million bushels of field crops grown in that province, to protect its butter, its cheese, its fruit, its cattle that are being exported to Great Britain. Then I come on to the province of Quebec, and we are here to protect its eighty-five million bushels of field crops, to protect its large exports of butter and cheese, to protect its 260 million dollars worth of foreign trade. I pass on to the maritime provinces, and we are here to protect the products of their farms, of their mines and of their fisheries. I pass on to the coast of Nova Scotia, with her unprotected sea coast of 5,600 miles, extending from the Bay of Fundy to the Straits of Belle Isle. It is said that the farmers of this country will not sanction any contribution towards the maintenance of a naval force, or in -keeping up a navy. I come back again, and I collect the surplus agricultural products of these various provinces, and I carry them down to the sea, and what do I find? I find that out of the 120 million dollars worth of agricultural products exported from the Dominion of Canada, no less than 101 million dollars worth go to that grand old country beyond the seas. In other words, of our total agricultural production exported from the whole Dominion, five-sixths pass down through the great lakes and along the various lines of railways, and are transported across the sea. It follows as a consequence that unless we can protect these lines of communication by which our exports proceed, we are absolutely at the mercy of some foreign power.
Then I will touch upon another aspect of the question. Our total trade last year was $650,000,000, an enormous amount. It is true a great portion of that is trade with the United States, but the balance is trade which has to seek an outlet across the seas, and which must be protected by Britain's navy. Then I come to the question of our fisheries. I find that in the Dominion of Canada our total fishery output is valued at 25 million dollars, of which we export 14 millions. We employ 84,000 men, and the capital invested in that industry is 15 million dollars. Is there an hon. gentleman in this House who would say that it is not of some importance to us to protect these fisheries, a large proportion of which is carried on upon the sea coast of our country? Speaker, the speeches delivered in the House to-day lead to the conclusion that the views held by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House on this question are not so divergent as on the surface they would appear to be. It may be assumed as an axiom that every member in this House and probably every citizen of Canada is loyal and true to the empire and prepared to support it in case of need. The time has gone by when the charge can be laid against any section of our people that they have not the interests of the British empire deeply at heart. I listened with pleasure and profit to the patriotic speeches delivered by the right hon. the Prime Minister and by the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). In this my first session in the Dominion parliament it was an inspiration to me to find that a debate of this importance could be raised to such a lofty plane and be so worthy of the Canadian nation. But, if we were to accept the words of the hon. member (Mr. Middlebro) in their literal sense we might well wince at the contract which he offers to us. He told us that we had the wheat fields of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, as well as the commerce of the other provinces of the Dominion to afford ample protection to. I would like to ask him how in the name of common sense there would be any chance of a hostile force reaching the interior of our country?
He said we had to protect the products of these provinces in transit.

Of course, when these products are in transit on the sea they might require protection, but so far as hostile invasion is concerned, with the exception of a narrow fringe on our Pacific and Atlantic coasts our country is impregnable. Even as to our coast line, it would seem to me that if we can protect our coal supplies a hostile fleet would be rendered powerless. It could not keep the sea. It has 'been asked during the debate what we are doing for the empire in comparison, for example, with New Zealand. I have seen it stated that New Zealand has given way to the panic which for a brief space spread over the empire and has offered one Dreadnought and expressed her readiness to supply another in case of need. Well, I have conversed with a good many persons from New Zealand in the last few years and the thought occurred to me that a country which has to borrow sc largely might perhaps be accused of

being generous when she ought to be just. But let us see if we are not doing something for the mother land. Is it nothing that we are providing at great expense to ourselves homes for the people of Great Britain, and thus relieving the congestion of population there? Is it not a fact that every workingman who finds a home in Canada ceases to be an expense to the mother country and becomes a source of strength to her in this part of the empire? What happened during the Boer war? In some respects that war was a blessing in that it demonstrated that England was not alone, but that her kindred beyond the seas were enthusiastic to rush to her aid and defend her interests. It was an object lesson never to be forgotten that Canada and the other parts of the British empire sent their sons to the veldts of South Africa to fight for the common welfare of the British empire. The resolution of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has been on the Order Paper since the first day of the session and hence the recent panic had nothing to do with its origin, but I think the House will agree with me that the existence of that panic had much to do with the interest taken in this discussion. The English are supposed to be the staidest people on earth, and yet it would almost seem that once in a decade or so they must get into some state of excitement, probably as a safety valve to keep them in their usually even frame of mind during the interval. There was a panic in England aroused by what was called the Battle of Dorking pamphlet, there was the Fashoda panic when some young French officer committed an indiscretion and the hot headed people and the excitable press of both nations were ready to fly at each other, but time has healed all that and to-day France and England live on terms of perfect amity. The present panic will, history repeating itself, be followed by others and so long as the instincts of the British people are as they are we may expect periods of excitement. To say anything detrimental of the British navy is a sore spot with every Englishman, and so whenever its supremacy is questioned there is likely to be excitement. Reading the history of the past we find there have been many scares of invasion in England. There was first the Armada, which miserably failed; then there was the Dutch invasion, but the Dutch navy, after a slight success and the British people found themselves, ceased to be a menace. Napoleon in the zenith of his power threatened to invade England, but it was but a threat, and so the present day scare of invasion will pass away and the British empire rise stronger and more glorious than ever. There is a matter which perhaps I am not competent to express an opinion on and it is this: Mr. WARBTTRTON.
We have heard much of Dreadnoughts and of the offers of some of the Australian colonies to contribute Dreadnoughts to the British empire. In the light of recent inventions and discoveries, it is just possible that the Dreadnought type of ship may not continue to be favoured very long. In our own recollection-and none of us are very old men-we can remember more than one change in the type of ships of war. In the early sixties, at the time of the civil war in the United States, the 'Merrimac' attacked an American fleet, which was supposed to be very powerful, and sank one or two ships, thus rendering obsolete all the fleets of the world at that time. During the Russo-Japanese war a few years ago, the Russian Admiral Marakoff placed his faith in the type of large cruisers which failed him, and now we have the very heavy type such as the Dreadnought. But many of the members of this House had the pleasure on Saturday last of listening to one of the greatest inventors of the day describing his recent discoveries, and speaking particularly of the airship. In view of the discoveries and inventions of the last twenty or thirty years, we cannot scoff at or belittle any invention. A few years ago any man who talked about transmitting messages by means of wireless telegraphy would have been looked on as a lunatic; and no one to-day can say that the warships of the future will not be airships. We know that the German government is experimenting along this line. In Cape Breton Dr. Bell and his associates are conducting similar experiments. It would not be at all beyond comprehension to suppose that one of these little airships might destroy a great ship of the Dreadnought type. So that we do not really know whether or not the vessels of this type are going to be permanent or not. It has seemed to me, ever since I devoted any thought to this question, that while we should take measures to protect our harbours on the sea coast, the real arm that we ought to strengthen is the military arm. I remember reading, in one of the speeches of Lord Roberts in Quebec last summer-and other men whose opinions are entitled to respect have said the same thing-that the great need of Great Britain to-day is not so much contributions of ships as contributions of soldiers to help her to fight her battles on land. She is very well able to take care of herself on the sea. The military arm of Canada has been greatly improved of late years until now we seem to have a real force. Possibly it may be necessary to spend more money on that force and on the protection of our seaports, and when we do that we do about all that it is possible for us to do. The British navy has held command of the seas for a century, and British statesmen say that there is no immediate probability

of her losing that command. So long as she can command the seas, the best assistance the outlying parts of the empire can render her is in strengthening the military arm and in protecting their own coasts.

At the same time, I feel that I would be derelict in my duty to my constituents if I did not endeavour to place before this House what I believe to be the views of the people of the city of Victoria and of the province of British Colum-bit upon this question. When the Pacific squadron was in existence, it had its headquarters at the town of Esquimalt, at a short 'distance from the city of Victoria, and practically a suburb of that city; so that the people of Victoria were brought into daily contact with the ofiicers and men, and had ample opportunity to judge of the ability and efficiency of the men composing His Majesty's navy. Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few remarks on this resolution and to give my views on its intrinsic value and importance. The resolution brought before the House by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is drawn in a very able and insidious manner. It appeals to our national pride and sets forth the fact that our resources are diversified and abundant. This is a broad admission that the country is in a far better financial situation than it was when the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) had the management of the Finance Department, and I am led to presume that this is the reason why such a resolution as the present one was never brought to the attention of parliament during the Conservative regime.
I am thankful to the sub-leader of the opposition for this disinterested and sincere acknowledgement, which bears testimony to the prosperity of Canada under Liberal administration.

I fully recognize the immense progress which has been achieved in all branches of public service, under the wise and able rule of our Liberal administration. I realize with pride and admiration the great success with which the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has administered the public money of this country, and I glory in the fact that with judicious economy he has had a considerable surplus over expenditure. I have no hesitation in saying that Canada has made a great step towards manhood and that the relations between our motherland and her greatest colony, are such as to let us anticipate, sooner or later, some change in the alliance between the two countries. I sincerely hope that a broad discussion of the most needed political changes will attract public attention to them and lend strength and importance to the movement in their favour because the political as well as the economical future of Canada must occupy a foremost place in the thoughts of those who have at heart the prosperity and greatness of our country.
What is the aim of the resolution now under consideration? Does it imply solely and directly the best interests of Canada or does it seek to afford military and naval help to England without any compensation? We have worked out, up to the present time, our own destiny and have enjoyed for many years past the utmost liberty, protected as we are by the British flag, I am happy to say. We have built up a great country and the energy and intelligence of the Canadian people have brought to completion gigantic enterprises which have evoked universal admiration. Our constitution, which derives its vitality from the fact that it is a shoot of British institutions grafted upon the federative form of the American constitution, gives us the utmost confidence in the final evolution of Canada into a great and prosperous country. I am an enthusiastic believer in the prophetic assertion of the right hon. leader of the Liberal party (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who, in a patriotic utterance, exclaimed that the twentieth century would be the century of Canada, as the nineteenth has been that of the United States. But in the face of all this, are we prepared to affirm that our country has attained such a state of development, growth and wealth as to justify the hazardous policy which the present resolution calls for? No, I do not think so and I venture to say that Canada has now reached that period of evolution in which the whirling and acute activity of her citizens, the demands of her industries and commerce, the requirements of a more perfect state of civilization, ought to impress on the mind of the leaders that it is their duty to direct all their attention and all the power at their disposal to obtaining for the people of Canada a moral, intellectual and material bettering.
The immense area of our land, the vast resources which it contains and the diversity of wants demanding help and redress are so many reasons calling for the action of parliament and the influence of our capital. Canada's wants, at present, Sir, are too pressing to allow of the idea that we can afford to expend millions by assuming the responsibilities involved in the present resolution. Have we not our great northwest, to which every year thousands of immigrants aTe flocking, willing to add by their labour and their intelligence to the wealth of the country, if their products can easily and economically reach the great markets* of the world? It is true that immense sums of money have already been spent in the direction of securing a sure and direct transportation, in building our two transcontinental railways, but is this sufficient, is that all that is to be done towards giving to our northwestern population the facilities and accommodations to which they are entitled?
We know that hundreds of thousands of bushels of grain are left in storage in the west each year owing to the lack of proper transportation capacity. This state of things cannot last and has to be remedied in the near future by the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. The northwestern settlers are clamouring for an adequate and economical transportation route and it is but fair to listen to their demands and to put them on an equal footing with their American northwestern competitors. The construction of the Georgian Bay Canal has occupied and occupies yet, I am proud to say, a prominent place in the Liberal programme, and I have such confidence and faith in the judgment and foresight of our leaders as to be firmly impressed with the idea that, instead of sacrificing millions in the construction of battleships and arming our coasts to flatter the imperialistic propensities of those whose erroneous patriotic ideas have misled them, provision will be made to ensure the construction of this great waterway. Millions will have to be spent for that purpose, it is true, but this expenditure is fully justified by the extraordinary results it will have in developing a vast area where flourishing cities will rise, giving life, comfort and happiness to millions of people.
Sir, Canada, it seems to me, has done something towards uniting the empire and in favour of imperialism, by the construction of our two transcontinental railways. The shortening of distances between England and her colonies beyond the seas, the great facilities offered to the mother land in giving her the benefit of using our railways to transport her troops and war material across America, on Canadian territory, in case of need, ought to be considered a generous contribution, on our part, to the building of the imperialistic edifice.

Sir, it is not, I humbly submit, by military strength alone that the English empire is to maintain its integrity, its high standing, its influence in the world and is to continue its glorious course, but it is also and mainly by giving to the people of the colonies that which is dearest to all, freer institutions and help in the great struggle for the general prosperity and comfort. Thus, England will be sure to find in a happy and contented population a true and strongly anchored loyalty. These are the stoutest links in the creation of a sound and high spirited imperialistic union. Have we not the experience of history to prove the truth of this? One of the most apparent'causes of the downfall of the great Roman empire and others was the inauspicious influence and hard ruling of militarism.
Sir, there are other battles to be fought than those carried on over land and sea by armed forces. The pacific war now going on amongst all civilized nations, or in other words the competition existing in commercial, industrial and educational matters is warning us to fully prepare ourselves by prompting public opinion with a proper policy if we wish to keep our place and rank in the present tremendous stress of human activity. ' The nation which is not progressing is retrograding ' says Lord Rosebery. If, sanguine in our adolescent capacity or erecting a false and tyrannical patriotism, we allow our national resources to be squandered, or our energy to be misused, we will have to bow down before the wisdom of really progressing nations, less endowed, may be, than we are, and confess our great error.
1 am in favour, Sir, of having a sufficient fleet for protecting our fisheries, and nothing more, and I am sure in saying this that I substantially reflect the opinion of my constituents.
We of the province of Quebec love the mother land and our loyalty cannot be questioned, I am sure, except perhaps by those who delight in high sounding formulas of patriotism and believe loyalty to consist merely in extravagant theories and unfair exigencies. We are, Sir, proud to be British subjects, always ready to fulfil our duties as such, but we are before all true and staunch Canadians.

At this late hour I do not wish to prolong the debate by any lengthy remarks. It appears to me, however, that several important questions have developed during the course of the discussion, and that whilst the original motion w'as couched in the mildest form possible, and calculated to bring before the attention of the House the question of naval defence and the urgency of matters imperial, with the condition of our forces as they are at present, still developments in Europe have brought about a new condition of affairs, Mr. G. A. TURCOTTE.
and it is necessary for this House, if possible, to give a stated opinion at an early opportunity as to its position, not only with regard to its own defence, but with regard to imperial defence. Let me point out that the lines of argument diverge. While the question of our own defence, is necessarily a portion of the imperial defence, the matter of imperial defence alone affects the situation particularly at the present moment. Several hon. members have laid out a plan as to what we should do in the future in the way of imperial defence and they have commended to us the plan of local defence such as they have adopted in Australia, which is 'a programme that requires a number of years to carry it out. I think there is no one in this House who will dispute the advisability of carrying out some such programme. But we find that peculiar conditions have arisen in the world's situation at the present moment, and that the mother country is threatened. While we are talking here, I am reminded of that old saying of Cicero: ' Gentlemen we deliberate, and Catiline is at the gate.' We are deliberating a great deal to-night as to what we should do six or seven years hence, but what the whole world is waiting to hear from us is a definite statement of what we are going to do in the present circumstances which have arisen in Europe.
Now, carrying out the idea first involved in naval defence for Canada, I do not see any reasons why we should not immediately institute some system of naval defence along the lines of torpedo boats, or torpedo destroyers, and idestroyer cruisers, which would be invaluable to us in case of war. A great many members suggest or imply that it would be impossible for us to build these at home. Now I do not wish to be considered local in any way, I have always taken a national or Canadian view of every subject; nevertheless, I may be permitted to say that within the riding which I have the honour to represent there is a shipyard wherein they) have launched ships over 500 feet in length, which is said to be the length of the Dreadnought. They have built ships, and they laid down the keel of one ship on the 26th of June last and launched her on the 1st of November, all complete, 375 feet long, 7,000 horse power, a 22 knot ship, with complete equipment, in that short time. If it was necessary for this government in ask them to supply four speedy cruisers 250 feet long, which could go through the canal, with a speed of 26 knots, I can assure you that I have it on the word of the men who designed these ships, and have built 22 steel ships' in the last four years, that it would be only a small matter for them to as-

semble the material, provide four ships and have them in the water by the 1st of October. The dock they use is 550 feet long, and would accommodate the Dreadnought.
I regret very much that as Canadians we have not fostered more this spirit of shipbuilding on the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. We are now manufacturing steel, the best steel in the world. We have two large steel plants. The steel plant at Sydney is a greater plant than any they have in Great Britain with larger and better furnaces, and in every respect a greater and larger steel plant. They have had there, for four or five years, a plate rolling plant to roll plates for ships, which they have housed away and never placed, on the foundation, because nothing has been done to encourage this most important industry. 1 feel that we should seriously, as a House of Commons, consider the advisability of adopting some system whereby shipbuilding would be encouraged in the maritime provinces, and also on the St. Lawrence and on the Pacific coast. We find that Germany, whom we have heard mentioned to-night, up till seven or eight years ago when she began to build her own ships, purchased her ships in England. Now there are in Germany eight ship yards where ships are built, and we are assured by a no less naval authority than the 'Naval Annual,' that they can lay the keels for 12 Dreadnoughts at once and complete them inside of 24 months if necessary. We find that Japan at one time purchased her warships from Great Britain, but she 'realized the importance of carrying on this industry in her own land and she has established shipbuilding yards in Japan 'where she buiids her own cruisers and her own commercial ships. Shipbuilding is a splendid enterprise, an enterprise that gives employment to a great number of men and it is the greatest national enterprise that a country can have; greater than the manufacture of guns and weapons of defence. We should undertake the work of building carriers because the money that is paid to foreign carriers to convey our products from Canada to Great Britain and other countries is a large sum which we should retain in our own country. As I pointed out we should immediately assume the position of establishing a local defence of our own. Our local defence 'should consist of torpedo boats and destroyers, and^ they could convoy our merchant ships, in case of war, to England and save them from the attacks of cruisers. I think we are all presumed to be at one upon that question. Now, let us come down to a more urgent matter, and that is the question of what we should do in the present situation to assist the motherland. We find that Great Britain at the present
moment is undergoing what some hon. gentlemen are pleased to call a music hall scare. I can assure hon. gentleman, from my knowledge of the facts and from the correspondence of business men in England who have a knowledge of the situation, that it is not a music hall scare. The fact is that the supremacy of Great Britain on the sea is challenged. Another nation has laid down within the last year, and will have laid down by April of this year, the keels of twelve Dreadnaughts. These Dreadnaughts will all be in commission by 1912 and Great Britain's supremacy as a world power will at that moment cease unless she can not only keep up with the naval programme of this rival nation but go farther. The burden of such an extensive enterprise as the building of so many warships at such an enormous cost has achieved such vast proportions that the English people, looking at it from purely a business standpoint, have said: ' It is cheaper for us to carry on a war now.' That is the position they have assumed. They have at the present time a naval preponderance over any other nation in Europe which they will lose in four or five years, and it is necessary for the national safety if they are going to have war that they shall have it now. They will have to spend a great deal of money in carrying on a war at a future date because war will be just as expensive then, if not more so, than it is now. They reason that if there is war now they will wipe the fleet of any nation that dares to challenge their supremacy off the sea and have peace again for the next twenty-five years. Those are sound logical reasons. We find that, following any great question of this kind we certainly have the music-hall element, but we have now the colonies making a response to the cry of war and offering aid to the empire. We know that this is an occasion for offering assistance to the empire. It is true that we offered the motherland the assistance of our men, and our rifles, and when we offered the services of our young men to the mother country we offered her a greater sacrifice, something that was even greater in monetary worth, if you like to put it in that way, than even the building of a Dreadnaught. We gave that freely at that time. We did not say that it was something that we would do only once or that we would continue from year to year, but we recognized the necessity of the situation and we rose to the occasion and offered our young men. They proved to the whole world that they were able to hold their own with the best troops in the world.
I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Cong-don) express the sentiments that he did.
I have had the opportunity of reading books about the Yukon, although I have never been there, and I had thought that

the men of the Yukon were men with red blood in their veins, men who were prepared to defend their country and to protect her soil. Instead of that the sentiments expressed by the hon. gentleman sounded very much as if the men in the Yukon, who sent him here, would be prepared, when war raised its horrid front to dash under the barn or take to the tall timbers. Now, we have discussed this question and a resolution has been presented by the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I trust that he will see his way clear to amend that resolution and I would ask if there is any self-respecting member of this House who is prepared to assert that we should only do a certain thing and go no farther. I feel satisfied that if war were declared the people of this country would be prepared to go to almost any length to maintain the integrity of the empire. Some of us realize that war is a terrible thing and my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has told us today that peace is almost impossible if England is in danger. If that great mother of nations,, the cradle of liberty, were threatened what would happen to us? Where would Canada be if England lost the command of the sea, if England's liberty were lost and if England became the colony of another nation? What would happen to Canada? Would not we also be penalized? If England lost the command of the sea and an indemnity were demanded would it not be the most natural thing in the world that the conquering nation would demand an indemnity in the shape of a colony? If, in the bargaining that goes on in the chancellories of Europe-and history tells us of many such bargains in the past in which colonies have been turned over to foreign nations-how would we look, having contributed nothing.to the common defence, if we found ourselves the colony of a European country? Whilst I agree with the right hon. First Minister that it is not necessary for us to enter into any obligations to contribute an annual sum, it is necessary for us to realize our duty to the country to which we belong and be prepared to offer not only men but money if necessary.

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much interest to the speeches delivered this afternoon and evening on the important subject matter of the resolution submitted by the hon. member for North Toronto. I should also say, as a new member of this House, that the manner in which the debate has been conducted, has exalted in my eyes the action of parliament, and that I am happy to form part of a body in which Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
subjects of such high importance are so treated.
I find that all the members who have spoken on the question have come to the identical conclusion that Canada should contribute to the defence of the Empire.
The latter portion of the resolution submitted by the hon. member for North Toronto reads as follows:
Canada should no longer delay in assuming her proper share of the responsibility and financial burden incident to the suitable protection of her exposed coast line and great seaports.
The hon. member's speech differs somewhat from his motion. He declared that not only should Canada have a navy to protect her shores and her large seaports, but that she should also help the empire in her wars with other countries. Should we. Sir, endorse such an expression of opinion? '
I love my country, Canada, and I know all she owes to Great Britain, but in such matters sentimental considerations may not be without danger. Before acting it is necessary to take into consideration the situation of Canada and all the special circumstances which surround the question.
It is said that Canada owes much to England. In what does the obligation consist? Especially in this, that England has granted us liberties which have enabled us to attain among the nations a position which is now beginning to be recognized as of importance.
It is also said that Canada owes much to England because the latter opens to us a very important market. True, but in this respect other considerations besides those of gratitude should be taken into account. When England first cast her eyes towards Canada it was not in a spirit of sacrifice but in a spirit of conquest, the object being to extend her commerce, her power, and her influence. It must not be forgotten that if the English market is open to Canada it is because England finds an advantage in purchasing Canadian goods. The advantage in this respect, being mutual there is cause for gratitude on both sides and the sentiment should be reciprocal.
It is said again that England has furnished us with millions which have helped to build our railways, to develop our territory, to excavate our canals and extend navigation to the interior of the continent. That is also true, but on the other hand Canada has proved a good field for the investment of English capital seeking dividends, and in this also we should be mutually grateful.
It is further contended that Canada should be grateful to England because of that military strength which has enabled us to develop in peace our natural wealth.

True again. But let us remember for what purpose England has sought to extend her influence to every part of the world. From east to west; it was because she desired to open to her sons-whose energy and gifts as a colonizing people cannot be denied-new fields in which those talents might be freely exercised and their rights undisputed. They have given to several countries of the world a progressive civilization and ideas of practical liberty, together with the advantages resulting from skilful administration and active trade. India, the Australian continent, New Zealand and several other countries are the living proofs of this. Thousands of England's sons come to Canada every year. We generously give them a peaceful home on the fertile western plains: they become sharers in our happiness and our wealth. And if on one hand we owe gratitude to England for the protection which has enabled us to develop our wealth, does not England also owe us some gratitude for the prosperity which her sons are to-day invited to share with us. It is right to place on each side of the balance that which pertains to each; doing that it will then be found that if England has done much for Canada, Canada, on the other hand, has done something for England.
All this leads me to say that it is not right to contend that Canada in the past has not done enough for Great Britain from a military point of view. The soldier who leaves his home and marches against the enemy offering his life for for his country, is a patriot whose heroism is highly praised. But what of the tiller of the soil whose corn feeds the armies and whose money supports them: is not his work at least as patriotic and as useful to his country? When we expended millions for the purpose of opening to agriculture the western fertile plains now becoming the granaries of the universe, were we dome nothing for the empire?
It has also been said that the amendment offered by the hon. the Prime Minister of Canada to the motion of the member for North Toronto, does not enunciate a well-defined policy nor entail prompt action in the creation of a navy. It is necessary in such a matter to act with great prudence and deliberation and to carefully consider all the circumstances surrounding us, before giving any exact and detailed statement of the policy which Canada should adopt.
We belong to the American continent over which prevails a principle called the Monroe doctrine. If I am not mistaken, that doctrine, much modified since its first enunciation, proclaims that no foreign power shall establish any new state nor make any new conquest on the American continent. Pre-existing colonies are allowed to remain
in the statu quo. Now, if we undertake today the creation of a navy in Canada and assume the risk of forcing this country into the militarist movement, it is to be feared that complications will naturally ensue. Our population is now seven millions, in twenty or forty years it may reach thirty or forty millions if the present rate of immigration is maintained. In a few years we will be a nation of some importance. Before entering into the military movement, we should weigh the inherent risks. Will other nations view our armaments with equanimity or indifference? Will the United States, ifor instance, witness without anxiety the growth, beside the vast power of England, of the military and naval establishments of Canada? Will Germany beheld without emotion the military organization of Canada upon the lines of an old time European power? I do not think so, for whenever a European state increases its means-of attack or defence, the diplomatic body becomes visibly perturbed, and cabinets study that important event which is invariably regarded as an act of aggression towards other countries.
What I have said does not imply that Canada should not adopt military measures for the defence of her coast and of her territory.
I may, with the hon. member for North Toronto, deplore that in the 20th century, and in our advanced stage of civilization, we should still be face to face with the military problem and obliged to expend such large sums of money for warlike "purposes. It is true that for two thousand years Europe has accepted the Christian rule and that the Decalogue proclaims to the nations 'Thou shalt not kill,' 'Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's goods.' Yet it cannot be denied that Christian nations who confess that creed still spend the greater part of their revenues and of their time in preparing for wars of defence or of aggression, for among them the idea of conquest still obtains. Defence naturally implies the idea of conquest on the part of the enemy. We must no doubt regret that in spite of civilization, nations cannot live in a manner more perfect and practice without fear of violence those principles of justice and equity which the Decalogue teaches, but Canada being a nation surrounded by other nations whose interests may conflict with her own, is bound to provide means of defence.
How should this be done? I say that the matter should be very carefully considered. The pretext of defence should not induce us to exhaust the sources of our energy. The expenditures must not be so great as to place us in the dilemma on the horns of which the European nations now find themselves. We must not for that purpose so

deplete our budget that nothing will remain to favour the emigration from Europe of those who might find here bread that is difficult to come by in their own overpopulated fatherlands. We must, therefore, act with prudence.
I question whether it would be wise to declare that Canada is ready to commence the immediate organization of a navy and to enter at one into the military movement.
Should Canada assert her intention to take immediate action on this matter, is it not to be feared that certain European consular bodies might take umbrage at this move of ours and should deem it advisable to rush conclusions in order to thwart this new element of contract ? Much could be said on this point. Let Canada organize a naval force to protect her coast line and her sea ports both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific; no one objects. But there is more to be be considered. If we say, in addition to the policy already laid down, that this force not only shall defend Canada, but must also take a part in Britain's wars, even those wars in which we are not concerned at all, then I say, Sir, that we are assuming much of a risk. My words are here nothing but the expression of many another one's opinion. When the day comes that we shall undertake all of Britain's wars, we shall incur the hostilities of other nations and open ourselves to their attacks. Their first care will be of course to neutralize our means of action by destroying our fleet, which we will be unable for many years to come to put on a sufficiently powerful footing to meet their attacks.
The attention of certain European countries might also be drawn upon us by this policy, and they might find it advantageous to set all possible means at play in order to keep our country from enlarging the scope of her influence, or to seize her, or to parcel her up in some way, before she has become too strong. Mr. Speaker, the bearing of the decision which we are called upon to take on the resolution of my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is all the more apparent that Canada is not at present threatened with war and in fact has none to fear, because, as I said before, we are protected by the Munroe doctrine. I admit, however, that this is not sufficient to allow us to sit down quietly. We are compelled by self-respect to do something to protect ourselves. Nevertheless, the Munroe doctrine imposes upon the United States the obligation of protecting us against the attacks of conquering spirit either from the east ot from the west. Is it in the interest of the United States to seize Canada ? I hardly believe it. Why should it ? Is it not getting along or. friendly terms with Great Britain ? Does not the occupation of Canada by Great Britain make it sure for them that Mr. EOT.
she would defend her colony against any foe from the east ?
I will not keep up this debate any longer by my observations. I say in short that I don't believe it is necessary that we should state in the resolution that such action must be immediate. The important point to assert is that everything which will be attempted in that way will be undertaken only after formal understanding with the British military authorities, in order that means of defence will be designed, which at the critical moment will offer adequate co-operation to the mother country. I do not think it is fair either to say that Canada has done nothing so far tc, help the mother country. If she did not contribute directly by her money, she did it in another way by the wohderful development she gave to her territory.
There is no immediate danger of hostilities. It is true that in the past few years, the leading nations of Europe have made what may be termed extraordinary expenditure towards the defence of their respective possessions. It is true that Britain who has so far held the undisputed supremacy of the seas, might be led to think at times, owing to the stand taken by other nations, that this supremacy is attempted to be wrested from her, but it must not be forgotten that Britain's superiority is acknowledged not only in her military force, but also in the strength of her diplomatic corps. She has been seen for a great many years to have nothing but internal wars to fight, such as that for instance, which she fought lately in South Africa. She has rather acted as a charming mediator between nations which did not always agree and which have waged war against each other. After all why be "more pessimist than Britain herself, when she does not foresee any immediate danger. What she wishes us to do, is to get up a naval force, which will be in a position to defend Canada when attacked.
Britain sticks to the policy which she formerly laid down towards her colonies. She says :	I give you full power of governing yourselves ; now that you are a nation, do as a free nation would.
This House is no doubt unanimous in its opinion that Canada should get up a naval force which will enable her to rank first among the nations, and thus command that respect which otherwise she would not command from those nations having hostile intentions against her. This unanimous feeling is the best evidence of the enlightened patriotism with which we are actuated.

Is it not a fact that since thenl these items have been excluded from the naval expenditure?

I could not say whether these items have been excluded or not from the naval expenditure of Great Britain. I am speaking of what happened at the imperial conference. It was stated that Canada was not expending anything on the fisheries protection service, and I thought it my duty to call the attention of the members of the conference to the fact that that

statement did not represent the situation exactly as it was. I do not know whether any change has been made since, but I am convinced that the naval expenditure of Great Britain to-day includes not only the construction of ships, but also the fisheries protection service, the hydrographic survey and the establishment of wireless telegraphic stations.
