speakeroldname: Mr. A. M. BEAUPARLANT (St. Hya cinthe).
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, in introducing his resolution, the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) laid down the principle that the physical or material power of a nation is the basic principle and the means by which it secures its development and its civilization, while preserving thereby its acquired wealth.
I agree with the hon. gentleman that such a principle will prevail so long as the present method of settling international disputes obtains.
But he will agree, I hope, that such is not the rule of equity applicable to conflicts arising between private individuals, between groups of population, or between cities and provinces.
He will agree that, because a man is endowed with greater physical strength than his neighbour, he is not entitled to claim larger rights before the courts of the country, or under the laws which govern the home administration in all civilized countries at least, and to the framing of which the hon. gentleman has himself contributed, in his capacity of an old parliamentarian, inspired no doubt by that pre-mordial and true feeling of wisdom and equity which governs all right-minded men.
I shall revert later on to this aspect of the question. Let us for a moment review the question, from the standpoint of the existing relations between the various nations.
Now, from that latter standpoint, I see no more immediate danger than opportunity, which should induce us to subordinate to that principle the national undertakings now under way.
Without stating it in explicit terms, the mover of the resolution before the House wishes to make a direct offer to the British Admiralty. His position in this regard coincides with that taken by a good Toronto paper, the ' News.'
That newspaper recently published two articles, one of which relating to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the other bearing on the question which is before us.
As a heading to the first of these two articles, there was a cartoon representing our Finance Minister extracting from the pocket of another individual representing Canada, certain sums of money intended ffjr a third individual personifying the Grand Trunk Pacific. The conclusion of tliat article as also that of the cartoon used as a heading was a blame directed to the Canadian government, on account of the expenditure incurred for an undertaking which, however, is of a national character. The second article had as a heading a cartoon representing New Zealand and Australia eager to bring to Great Mr. BRODEUR .
Britain those pretty boats called ' Dreadnoughts.' Then, in the background stood an individual representing Canada, viewing that spectacle, motionless and impassive.
The conclusion of that second article and the accompanying cartoon was a blame inflicted to Canada for hesitating to incur the necessary expenditure so gratifying to Great Britain.
Now, without applying too strictly the principle that ' well-ordained charity begins at home,' which savours of egotism, I disapprove of this newspaper who shares in the opinion of the member from North Toronto trying to subordinate our own national undertakings to an undertaking which is to be carried on a territory altogether different from our own.
And should some overzealous minds be scandalized at my statement, let me remind them that the first Lord of the British Admiralty, Sir Reginald McKenna, has himself recently stated that the British navy was so far ahead of its rivals that there was no immediate danger. Closer to us, one of the leading minds in this House, the member for South York, made from his seat in this House, on the 11th of February, 1907, the following statement:
' I am one of those who believe in Canada first and empire next.' With the exception of the member for the Yukon, no member of this House has made a more categorical statement.
The ' Saturday Review,' of London, stated at the same date, that it was high time for Canada to think of using her own treaty-making power.
Therefore, I do not stand alone here in protesting against imperialism and militarism. As to us, French Canadians, our adherence to British interests is grounded on reason, which is more lasting than mere sentiment, as may be gathered from the history of the American colonies. Those who would rather make a gift to Great Britain than coming to her assistance in time of need, evidently abdicate the faculty of discussing certain events which have arisen in the past history of other nations and may arise here in the future, and I for one do not wish to divest myself of that privilege.
Our sympathies are grounded on the proverbial British fair play, evidences of which Great Britain has given us in the parliamentary system granted to us under the successive Acts passed in 1774, 1791, 1840, and 1867.
Perhaps the most regrettable event which has ever marred our relations with Great Britain was the violent character of the means resorted to in order to quell the insurrection of 1837, at a time when Great Britain had in her power and at her mercy a few powerless insurgents. Even from the standpoint of British diplomacy, toleration

and humanity would have been the wiser course to follow; and one would have first to eradicate from the hearts of the Canadian people an inborn feeling, should one expect these events to be mentioned without stirring up some painful recollections.
But between Great Britain and us there has been laid the foundation of generous compensations. We have learned how to forget, in view of the liberal treatment above alluded to.
Such adhesion on my part, however, restricted it may be, but resting on the above stated grounds, may perhaps carry more weight with and be more acceptable to those who hear me, than a sweeping and unqualified approval, the grounds of which would be likely to breed suspicion or could not be accounted for.
With the above qualifications thus frankly stated, I may now examine the question before the House.
One of the first points that call our attention in the resolution before us is the financial liability involved in the application of the principle extolled therein.
The combined cost of the British Army and Navy is in round numbers $400,000,000 every year. .
Is Canada prepared and willing to contribute her proportionate share to such an expenditure to be incurred every year?
The surpluses accumulated within the last few years are no longer sufficient to meet our national undertakings. While in England, recently, our Minister of Finance had to negotiate a loan for the purposes of the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Georgian Bay Canal, a scheme which is perfectly practicable in a near future, may probably call for further loans.
I am far from posing as a financial expert, but I may state here that I do not see any other means of meeting the foreshadowed expenditures than by adding to our Customs Tariff, at least the 3:07 per cent taken off, within the last twelve years, a reduction which I think has benefited the whole people of Canada, or else by raising some special taxation.
Is the contribution to the Imperial Navy of such an opportunity that the Liberal Government of Canada should believe themselves justified in changing their fiscal policy, approved of by the electors of this country at the polls at four general elections, and on grounds whiqh have not been submitted to the consideration of the Canadian electorate?
On the other hand, are the citizens of Toronto, Hamilton, London or Sarnia more willing than the citizens of Montreal, St. Hyacinthe, Three Rivers or Quebec to submit to that special taxation or to borrow from Great Britain in order to make a gift to Great Britain.
Still, I for one am willing to make all those sacrifices, but only for the purposes of the creation of a navy to remain under our own exclusive control and for us alone, and by means of which we may, when opportunity offers, lend our help to Great Britain whose prestige is for us a guarantee of security.
Coming in such a way to the assistance of England would be more useful and more satisfactory to us, the more so as we should then avoid pledging our future.
Although in principle I am disinclined to give my support to any expenditure of a military character, still one must take into consideration the conditions of equilibrium between the different nations, and so long as those conditions are not settled in a more desirable way I am willing to give my consent to any necessary sacrifices for the protection of the country.
Without entering here into the question of universal peace, a system which is by no means impracticable, but which may for a long time remain a speculative question, one may at least express the opinion that, should the different nations devote to that purpose one half of the sacrifices made and efforts put forth to secure the triumph of their respective claims without always inquiring as to the proportion of equity they contain, they would secure greater advantages and more wealth than are reaped by the victorious nations themselves from present conditions. I am far from pretending to be familiar with universal history, but I am free to confess that should anyone be able to single out even among the most powerful nations one solitary example of a people for which war has not proved the worst of evils, he would reveal to me a fact, the existence of which, as a modest student of history, I have never had the least suspicion. Victory and even conquest which is sometimes the sequel of victory, constitute but a partial compensation for losses resulting from the clashing of navies and armies.
England and France are the two countries which have played the most prominent part during our era. Stupendous as has been the work of England, as we all readily admit, I do not think that a single decade has elapsed in her history without her having had a war to sustain.
As to France, after so many quarrels and struggles, she does not own to-day a single square meter of territory more than she possessed 1,400 years ago, under her fourth king.
But such is not the question we have to examine now, at a time when some feverish individuals seem to hear rumours of conflicts, which is always an opportunity for starting a movement of a similar nature to the one which is now in full swing. One must take into consideration the pre-

sent conditions of settling conflicts between nations.
So long as powerful nations shall not take a serious and effective lead in compulsory national arbitration; so long as it shall be considered proper to submit to a disinterested third party and to no other the dispute arising between two private individuals, while refusing to apply the same measure of justice to the quarrels between nations; so long as governments whether democratic or autocratic, shall bind their subjects by laws to which they themselves refuse to submit; so long as it is conceded that there is more of right and justice in a fourteen-inch gun than in an eight-inch gun; so long as right shall be might in international matters, we are bound to make the sacrifices necessary for our own protection, but let the fruits of those sacrifices remain under our own control. That is the most rational method we can adopt of helping Great Britain and it is in the interest of both parties that we, a nation in course of formation, should avoid the less reasonable method of offering sums of money to the British nation whose energetic efforts have been accumulating for centuries such colossal wealth.
My conception of patriotism may differ from that of several members of this House. There enters a good deal of narrow egotism in the ordinary feeling called by that name. It consists in a sort of nepotism of family preference applying to the nation and which, it seems to me, should make way for the far more attractive humanitarian concept. After such a declaration on my part, which, I hope, will be considered sincere, I will not, I suppose be accused of national prejudice.
On the contrary, I am desirous, in all loyalty and with the assurance that my action will not be misconstrued, to offer friendly co-operation to the sons of that British race who in two leading events of their history and in the evolution of their nation, have secured political and civil liberty at less heavy a price than another great nation in an identical attempt made later on.
The Anglo-Saxon in Canada is the equal of those of his race, both in England and in the United States; he is proud of his past and desirous of casting aside all that may impede his progress; there is nothing to prevent our working together, our interests and aims being in the main identical.
It has often been pointed out that there are between us differences of language, creed and tradition, but with similar differences of race, small countries such as Switzerland and Belgium, who have neither our great rivers or extensive plains, have secured the respect of the world at large and a prominent position in industrial, mental and moral development.
The present question has no reference to matters of language, creed or tradition, it Mr. BEAUPAELANT.
refers exclusively to the nature, conditions and advantages of our political relations, and to the control to be exercised over any given portion of the empire. In this I feel sure that my opinion will be shared by the majority of English-speaking members in th is House. A people numbering among its leaders such men as Gladstone and Sir H. Campbell-Bannerman, who so ably advocated the cause of home rule for others, cannot object to the principle of home rule when applied to ourselves.

speechtext:
The suggestions which have been made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition are such as can be accepted by this side of the House, and I have no objection to adding the words, so that the resolution will read as follows:
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of a Canadian naval service.
With regard to the paragraph stating what we have already done in alleviating the burden of the British taxpayer, there is no objection at all to striking that out. I therefore move the amendment in the following form:
That all the words after ' that ' be struck out and the following substituted thereto:
This House fully recognizes the duty of the people of Canada, as they increase in numbers and wealth, to assume in larger measure the responsibilities of national defence.
The House is of opinion that under the present constitutional relations between the mother country and the self-governing dominions, the payment of regular and periodical contributions to the imperial treasury for naval and military purposes would not, so far as Canada is concerned, be the most satisfactory solution of the question of defence.
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial n^vy, along the lines suggested by the admiralty at the last imperial conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the empire and the peace of the world.
The House expresses its firm conviction that whenever the need arises the Canadian people will be found ready and willing to make any sacrifice that is required to give to the imperial authorities the most loyal and hearty co-operation in every movement for the maintenance of the integrity and honour of the empire.

Amendment agreed to, and motion as amended agreed to.
